clinicalPearls: Presents as multiple flat-topped, skin-coloured, wart-like papules on the dorsa of the hands and feet, wrists and forearms
It is an autosomal dominant disorder allelic to Darier disease, both caused by variants in ATP2A2, which encodes the SERCA2 calcium pump
The papules resemble plane warts but are non-viral and tend to be symmetrical and persistent
Punctate keratoses or pits on the palms and soles and nail changes may accompany the acral papules
Because it is allelic to Darier disease, some individuals or families show overlapping features, so a personal and family history of Darier disease is relevant
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and a church-spire papillomatosis without the acantholytic dyskeratosis of florid Darier disease
Management is largely cosmetic with keratolytics, cryotherapy or other destructive methods, and reassurance about the benign nature
reference.pathophysiology: Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf is caused by variants in ATP2A2, encoding the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase isoform 2 (SERCA2), which pumps calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum and maintains the calcium gradients needed for normal keratinocyte adhesion and differentiation. Impaired SERCA2 function disturbs desmosomal assembly and epidermal differentiation, producing focal hyperkeratotic, papillomatous acral papules. Because Darier disease results from variants in the same gene, the two are allelic, and the milder acral phenotype can coexist with or occur in families affected by Darier disease.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and church-spire papillomatosis without prominent acantholysis
Assessment for coexisting Darier disease features
Dermoscopy to distinguish from viral warts
Nail and palmoplantar examination for associated changes
redFlags: Rapid change or ulceration in an individual lesion suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Widespread florid disease indicating overlap with Darier disease
Diagnostic uncertainty from atypical or verrucous lesions
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and chronic with no malignant potential; lesions persist and may slowly increase in number, and the impact is essentially cosmetic.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating the papules as recalcitrant viral warts
Overlooking the allelic relationship with Darier disease and its family history
Over-treating benign acral papules with aggressive destruction and scarring
Failing to reassure the patient about the benign nature of the condition
management: Reassurance that lesions are benign with no malignant potential, so treatment is for cosmetic reasons only
Cosmetic destruction of troublesome papules with cryotherapy, ablative laser or electrodesiccation
Topical keratolytics and retinoids, with oral retinoids reserved for extensive disease, recognising the often limited response
Assess for coexisting Darier disease features given the shared ATP2A2 (SERCA2) mutation
Genetic counselling and pedigree analysis given autosomal dominant inheritance
